unit.title: Provide financial and business performance information

summary: This unit teaches you to provide financial and business performance information that managers can trust and use. You will learn to find out what information each user needs, gather and check data from the ledger and operating systems, work out ratios, trends, variances and key performance indicators, present the results clearly with commentary, protect confidential information, deliver it on time and review whether the reporting is useful.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for supervisors and managers in Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools, agencies and public bodies who prepare, check or present information about how the organisation is performing. The information may be financial (sales, costs, profit, cash) or about the business more widely (customers served, complaints, occupancy, staff turnover, time to deliver).

**Performance information** is useful only if it is **relevant** (it helps a decision), **accurate**, **timely**, **clear** and **protected**. Your job is to get the right figures to the right person, in a form they can understand, in time for them to act, and to be honest about what the figures do and do not show.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workplace
rows: Find out which decisions each manager makes and agree the measures, sources, format, frequency and deadline.
Collect figures from the ledger, sales system, payroll and operating records, on time and complete.
Reconcile systems, test for odd movements, check formulas, keep a trail back to source.
Calculate ratios, percentages, trends, variances, unit costs and KPIs, and compare with budget, last year and similar organisations.
Choose the right table or chart, write a short commentary, and design reports and dashboards for the reader.
Keep personal and confidential data safe, release it only to those entitled, and never hide or distort results.
Meet deadlines, give early figures marked as unchecked when needed, answer queries and correct errors.
Ask users what they use and what they miss, and improve or drop measures.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with scenarios and calculations (margins, ratios, growth, variances, unit costs, rates).
A **written paper** with short answers (terms and short sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Group practical tasks**: checking and analysing a data pack and building a one-page dashboard with commentary; and interviewing managers to agree information specifications and briefing them on results.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice. Write the formula, show the figures, then state the answer with its unit (J$, %, days, ratio).
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Do not start from the data you have. Start from the **decisions** each user must make. A general manager deciding whether to open a new branch needs different information from a front-desk supervisor deciding who works on Saturday. The decision sets the **level of detail**, the **time span** and the **frequency**.

head: Level
Typical user
Typical decisions
Information
rows: Today's and this week's work: rosters, stock to reorder, queues
Detailed, daily or weekly, mostly non-financial
This month's and quarter's results against budget; costs; staffing
Direction: new branch, loans, prices, investment
Highly summarised, quarterly or yearly, trends, forecasts, risks

head: User
What they want to know
rows: Profit, return on their investment, growth
Can the organisation repay on time? Cash, liquidity, debts, security
Were funds used as agreed? Were targets met? Value for money?
Job security, pay, how the organisation is doing
Service quality, waiting times, use of public money

blocks.h: Finding out what a manager needs

flow: List the users and the decisions each one makes
Meet each user and ask open questions: What decisions do you make? How often? What do you need to know to make them? What do you do now?
Read the business plan and budget, so the measures match the organisation's goals
Draft an **information specification** for each user
Check the draft with the user, and agree what is possible with the systems and staff available
Agree who may see sensitive information, such as pay
Agree a review date (for example after three months), because needs change

blocks.p: If a director says 'give me everything about costs', do not hand over everything. Ask which cost decisions she must make (a price rise? cutting overtime? a contract?) and supply the cost information for those.

head: Item
Example (production manager)
rows: Waste in kilograms, and as a % of material used
One-page table with last week's figure, target and last year

head: Source
Examples
rows: General ledger, sales and purchase ledgers, budget, cash book, payroll
Till or point-of-sale system, stock system, check-in or booking system, time records, complaints log, staff records
Industry association surveys, published statistics, competitor prices, customer surveys, bank statements, supplier statements

ul: List what each report line needs and **where it comes from**. Agree with the owner of each source when the data will reach you after month end.

Make sure the data covers the **whole period** (cut-off). Items such as the last day's sales, or fuel used in the last week of the month for which the invoice arrives next month, should be included, or estimated and noted.
Use the **same definitions** each time (for example whether sales include GCT; whether staff costs include employer contributions).

head: Check
How it is done
Example
rows: Agree the total in one system to the same total in another
Ticket revenue in the ledger J$41,250,000; ticketing system J$41,520,000; difference J$270,000, which must be traced
Compare each figure with last month, last year and budget; query large or odd changes
A line that is ten times its usual size may be a keying error
Check a total with a calculator
Review spreadsheet formulas, ranges and links; lock formula cells; keep a change log
A total that leaves out a row
A colleague checks the key figures
Another member of staff agrees the dashboard to the ledger
Keep notes of sources and adjustments so each figure can be traced to source documents
Reference each reported figure to a ledger account or report

blocks.note: If a cost has been coded to the wrong account, **correct the coding** and use the corrected figure. Do not report a figure you know to be wrong, and do not simply adjust the report without fixing the ledger.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Worked example: a difference between two systems

blocks.p: The ledger shows ticket revenue of J$41,250,000 and the ticketing system shows J$41,520,000. Difference = J$41,520,000 − J$41,250,000 = **J$270,000**. The preparer does not guess. She finds that one depot's weekend takings were banked on 1 July and entered in the system on 30 June but in the ledger on 1 July (a cut-off difference). She corrects the period, explains the adjustment in her notes and reports the agreed figure.

ul: Lock formula cells and protect sheets.
Allow each person to change only their own data cells, and keep a log of changes.
Keep one master copy and a back-up; name versions clearly.
Check totals against the ledger before the report is issued.

sections.title: Analysing performance: ratios and unit costs

blocks.p: Ratios turn many figures into a few that can be compared over time, with budget and with other organisations. Learn the formulas, work the sums twice, and always ask **what the figure means** and **why** it moved.

**Why use margins?** Compare two branches. Branch A has sales of J$30,000,000 and net profit of J$2,400,000 (8%). Branch B has sales of J$16,000,000 and net profit of J$1,600,000 (10%). Branch A earned more J$ profit, but Branch B earned more on each dollar of sales.
**Percentage points.** If gross margin falls from 36% to 33%, it has fallen by **3 percentage points** (not 3%).

blocks.h: Liquidity: can the organisation pay its short-term debts?

ul: A current ratio below 1 means current liabilities are more than current assets: the organisation may struggle to pay on time.
The quick ratio **leaves out stock** because stock may take time to turn into cash. A big gap between the two ratios means the organisation relies on stock to cover its debts.
A very high ratio can mean cash or stock is sitting idle.

blocks.p: Compare debtor days with the credit terms offered. If terms are 30 days and debtor days are 35, customers are paying 5 days late on average.

blocks.note: Use the correct denominator. Cost per **trainee who completed** divides by those who completed, not by those who started. Percentage growth divides by last year, not this year.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **variance** is the difference between the budgeted figure and the actual figure. Variance % = (actual − budget) ÷ budget × 100.

ul: A cost over budget is **adverse**; a cost under budget is **favourable**. For income the reverse is true: income above budget is favourable.
Report the cause (price, volume, timing, error), not just the size.

blocks.note: Always say what the figure shows and why it matters. A ratio shows that something has changed but not **why**. Investigate the cause before acting.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Trends, comparisons, KPIs and non-financial measures

ul: A **single month** may be affected by a one-off event (a storm, a big order, a strike). A **twelve-month trend** is more reliable.
Plot figures over time (a line graph) and look at direction, size and sudden jumps.
Beware of **seasonality**: a Jamaican hotel's revenue is usually lower in September and October than in the winter high season. Compare September with September of last year, not with August.
If sales rise 15% but gross profit in J$ stays the same, the **margin has fallen**: look for higher costs, discounts or a change in the sales mix.

head: Compare with
Shows
Caution
rows: Where you are better or worse than comparable organisations
Compare like with like: size, market, methods

blocks.p: A **KPI** is a measure of how well an important objective is being met. A good KPI is **relevant** to a goal, **clearly defined**, has a **target**, a **named owner**, a **source of data** and a **reporting frequency**. A few well-chosen KPIs are better than dozens of figures.

head: Department
Example KPIs
rows: Food and beverage in a hotel
Food cost % (food cost ÷ food sales); revenue per cover; guest satisfaction score; labour cost % of sales; waste per week
% of invoices paid within 30 days; debtor days; month-end closed by working day 5
% of calls answered within the target time; complaints per 1,000 transactions
Staff turnover %; time to fill a vacancy; absence rate
% of applications processed within the standard time; cost per case; satisfaction with service

ul: **Lagging indicators** show what has already happened (this month's sales, profit).
**Leading indicators** give early warning of what is likely to happen (quotations sent, bookings for next month, enquiries).
Managers need both: leading indicators to act early, lagging indicators to confirm results.

blocks.p: Money figures often arrive after the month ends and do not explain **why** results happened. Non-financial measures can be collected daily and give early warning.

head: Sector
Examples
rows: Occupancy = rooms sold ÷ rooms available (2,325 ÷ 3,100 = **75%**); average daily rate (ADR) = room revenue ÷ rooms sold (J$27,900,000 ÷ 2,325 = **J$12,000**); revenue per available room (RevPAR) = room revenue ÷ rooms available (J$27,900,000 ÷ 3,100 = **J$9,000**, which also equals ADR × occupancy: J$12,000 × 75%)
Attendance rate; examination pass rate; class sizes
Waiting time; patients seen per day; missed appointments
Complaints per 1,000 transactions; calls answered within target; repeat customers
Staff turnover; absence; energy and water use; time to deliver

blocks.p: A **balanced scorecard** looks at performance from four perspectives so that managers do not watch only profit:

head: Perspective
Question
Example measure
rows: How do we look to owners and funders?
What must we be good at?
Training days per person; staff turnover

blocks.p: A hotel with good profit this month may be hiding falling guest satisfaction that will cut future bookings; high occupancy at heavy discounts may earn little profit. Using both financial and non-financial information shows both current results and the drivers of future results.

If a report includes a forecast (for example year-end profit), it must show the **main assumptions** behind it (sales growth, prices, costs, exchange rate) so managers can judge it. Show how the forecast changes if the assumptions change.

blocks.h: The limits of ratios and trends

ul: They depend on the **quality of the data** behind them.
They look at the **past**, which may not repeat.
A **single period** can be distorted by one-off events.
Comparisons with other organisations are unfair if they differ in size, methods or market.
A ratio shows that something changed, not **why**. Ratios should prompt questions, not give final answers.

blocks.h: Match the presentation to the reader

ul: A **busy director** wants a one-page summary and the exceptions.
A **board whose members are not accountants** needs a few clear charts and key terms explained simply.
A **supervisor** needs short, current, practical figures for the job in hand.
Use the same **units, periods and layout** on every page, so figures can be compared quickly.

flow: One-page summary: main results, the three or four issues needing decisions, recommendations
Dashboard: agreed key measures against target and last year, with red, amber and green flags
Charts and tables for the main measures, with commentary beside each
Commentary: what moved, why, the effect, and what is being done
Detailed schedules in an appendix for those who want them
Notes on sources, assumptions and any figures not yet checked

head: Purpose
Best display
Notes
rows: Show all months, same scale each time
Show how a total splits into parts
Pie chart (few slices) or stacked bar
Define what red, amber and green mean

blocks.note: A bar chart whose vertical axis starts at J$9,000,000 instead of zero makes a small rise look huge. Start axes at zero for bars, label axes and units, and use the same scale from month to month, so the chart does not mislead.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Exception reporting** shows only items outside agreed limits, so a busy manager looks first where it matters.
**RAG** colours: **red** is outside the tolerance and needs action; **amber** is near the limit; **green** is on target. The limits for each colour are agreed in the specification.

blocks.p: Tables alone do not tell managers what to do. A short written **commentary** explains the **cause** of each key movement. A good commentary line says: what changed, by how much, why, what effect, and what action is proposed. Example: 'Gross margin fell from 36% to 33% (3 percentage points) because supplier prices rose in May and discounts were given to win two large orders. Management proposes to review prices in July.' Use plain language and explain technical terms.
A **dashboard** linked to the accounting system gives managers current figures on demand. It still needs checking and clear definitions: a dashboard fed with wrong data is quickly wrong.

When a manager must choose between options (for example keeping cleaning in-house or contracting it out), give the financial information (full cost of each option over several years, GCT at the current rate where it applies, one-off costs, assumptions) and the non-financial information (quality, risk, effect on staff, rules such as public procurement rules). Present a one-page comparison, list the risks, and state what is uncertain. Set out the evidence fairly; the manager makes the decision.

ul: Know which information is **confidential**: staff pay and personal details, customer account data, prices and contracts, results not yet released to the board or the public.

Follow the organisation's information policy and the general aims of the **data protection law**: personal data is used only for a proper purpose, kept to what is needed, kept accurate and kept secure.
Give each user only what they are **authorised** to see. Report pay by department totals rather than named salaries unless the user is entitled to see names.
Store reports in folders with access controls; password-protect spreadsheets holding personal data.
Send reports through the organisation's secure systems, **never from personal email**, and check the recipient list before sending.
Collect printed copies from the printer at once and shred them when no longer needed.
If someone asks for information they are not entitled to, **decline politely and refer them to the authorised manager**.
Report any breach (a report sent to the wrong person, a lost laptop) immediately under the policy.

blocks.p: Information must be honest and complete. If a manager asks you to leave out a large loss so the quarter 'looks better', or to move the date of invoices so that income falls in the current period, **you must not do it**. Keep the true figure, explain politely that you must report accurately, and report the request to a more senior person (the finance director, the audit committee or internal audit) if it continues.

head: Pressure
Right response
rows: 'Leave out that loss for the board.'
Keep it in; refer the request upward
Refuse to alter the dates; record transactions in the right period
'Give me everyone's salary, I want a feel for the numbers.'
Give only what the role is entitled to; refer him to the authorised manager
'Just send the file to my private email.'
Use the secure system; follow the information policy

blocks.note: Honest reporting protects you, your managers and the organisation. Information that has been distorted leads to bad decisions, and the person who prepared it is answerable.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Timeliness, responding to users and reviewing the system

ul: Agree **deadlines** with users and keep to them. A monthly pack that reaches managers 25 days after month end arrives too late for them to act on it.
Shorten the month-end process: agree cut-off times with data owners, use standard templates, link the dashboard to the accounting system.
When a manager needs a figure by noon but full checks take two days, give an **early figure clearly marked as unchecked or provisional**, and follow with the checked figure.
A **flash report** of a few key figures within three working days gives early warning while the full pack follows.
Answer queries promptly, politely and with evidence.
If a user queries a figure, check the source, reply, and correct it if it is wrong.
If you find an error after issue, tell the users promptly, issue the corrected figure, and record the cause. Do not wait for someone to find it.
Offer a short briefing for managers who need help understanding the pack.

blocks.p: Reporting should be reviewed with its users, at least yearly and when needs change.

head: Question
How to find out
rows: Ask which items they use and which they miss
If managers never use eight of twenty measures, agree with them to drop or replace those measures
Is it on time and accurate?
Ask managers whether they could act on it; watch where they ask for help
Time spent preparing it compared with its use

blocks.p: A pack that is 40 pages long, three weeks late and hard to use should be cut to a summary page, a dashboard and a few pages of commentary, with detail in an appendix or on request. Use exception reporting. Agree the key measures with each manager, and review the new format after three months.

ul: start from the decision, and say how needs differ between operational, tactical and strategic users;
list the users of performance information and what each wants to know;
write an information specification (measure, source, format, frequency, deadline, access);
gather data from the ledger and operating systems, including cut-off items;
check accuracy by reconciling, testing for odd movements, checking formulas and keeping a trail to source;
calculate gross and net margins, current and quick ratios, debtor, creditor and stock days;
calculate growth, averages, cost per unit, rates per 1,000, staff turnover and variance %;
use trends, seasonality, budgets, last year and benchmarking fairly;
choose KPIs and non-financial measures, and explain leading and lagging indicators and the balanced scorecard;
choose the right chart, avoid misleading axes and use exception reporting and RAG;
write a clear commentary that explains causes;
protect confidential and personal data, and refuse to distort or hide results;
deliver on time, mark early figures as unchecked, answer queries and correct errors;
review the information system with its users.

terms: Financial and non-financial information that shows how well the organisation is doing
A record of each measure, its source, format, frequency, deadline and who may see it
Comparing two sets of records to make sure they agree
A record that lets a figure be traced back to its source documents
Making sure transactions are recorded in the correct period
Current assets less stock, divided by current liabilities
The difference between budget and actual
The simple difference between two percentages
A measure of how well an important objective is being met
A measure that gives early warning / a measure of results already achieved
A set of measures under four headings: financial, customer, internal process, learning and growth
A screen or page showing key measures together, often as charts
Reporting only items outside agreed limits
Red, amber, green: status colours for measures against target
A short early report of a few key figures
The law that sets how personal data may be used, kept and protected

c1.title: Information needs at a hardware chain in Mandeville
c1.text: A hardware chain with branches in Mandeville and Savanna-la-Mar employs a new management accountant, Shanelle. The owner wants to know whether the chain is growing and profitable. The Mandeville branch manager wants to know each morning which stock lines have run low. The chain's bank, which lent money for stock, wants to know whether the chain can repay on time. Last month the chain's sales were J$15,000,000, cost of sales was J$9,600,000 and net profit was J$1,350,000. The till system holds each day's sales, and the accounts are closed monthly.

c2.title: Checking the quarterly report at a bus operator in St Thomas
c2.text: A bus operator in St Thomas is preparing its quarterly report. Ticket revenue in the ledger is J$41,250,000, but the ticketing system shows J$41,520,000. Fuel was used in the last week of June, but the supplier's invoice arrives in July. Several depot clerks add data to one shared spreadsheet that feeds the dashboard. The preparer, Garfield, must be able to show where every reported figure came from.

c3.title: A supermarket's figures in Portmore
c3.text: A supermarket in Portmore reports sales rising from J$52,000,000 to J$58,500,000 over the year. Credit sales to restaurants are J$29,200,000 a year and receivables are J$2,800,000. Current assets are J$5,400,000 (including stock of J$1,800,000) and current liabilities are J$3,000,000. The budget for electricity was J$3,200,000 and the actual cost was J$3,456,000.

c4.title: A finance committee pack at a municipal corporation in Portland
c4.text: The Portland municipal corporation's finance committee receives a monthly performance pack from the finance officer. Councillors are not accountants. The pack includes a dashboard with red, amber and green flags, a chart of how the budget is split among departments, and a measure of complaints per 1,000 service users. Councillors say the commentary is often missing.

c5.title: Pressure on a reporting officer at a property company in Montego Bay
c5.text: A reporting officer at a property company in Montego Bay prepares the quarterly pack for the board. A manager asks her to change the dates on invoices worth J$1,200,000 so that the income falls in this quarter instead of next. The officer also wants to work on a spreadsheet of customer accounts at home and considers emailing it to her personal account. After the pack is issued she finds that one figure on the dashboard is wrong by J$450,000.

questions.q: How do the information needs of the owner and the Mandeville branch manager differ?
o: The owner needs detailed daily figures; the manager needs yearly summary totals
Both need the same monthly profit report, but in a different colour
Owner: summarised, longer-term results. Manager: detailed daily stock figures
The owner needs only non-financial figures; the manager needs only financial ones
questions.why: Needs follow from the decisions each person makes. An owner judges direction and profit, using summarised results over months. A branch manager decides what to reorder today and needs detailed, current stock figures.

questions.q: Which would be a suitable external source for benchmarking the chain's gross margin?
o: Trade association data for similar hardware businesses
The chain's own till system records for the past year
The chain's bank statements for all three branches
The staff roster for the Mandeville branch this month
questions.why: External sources let you compare with similar organisations. The till system, bank statements and staff rosters are internal sources and cannot show how the chain compares with others.

questions.q: The branch manager needs stock availability every morning, but the accounts close only monthly. What should Shanelle do?
o: Ask the manager to wait for the monthly accounts to be finished before ordering any stock
Close the whole accounts system every day so that all figures are always current
Send the owner's monthly profit report to the manager on the first day of each week
Take daily stock figures from the stock system and money figures from the monthly accounts
questions.why: The frequency of information should match the decision. Daily stock decisions need data from the operating system; profit decisions use the monthly accounts. One source is not forced to serve every purpose.

questions.q: Last month the chain made a net profit of J$1,350,000 on sales of J$15,000,000. What is its net profit margin?
questions.why: Net profit margin = net profit / sales x 100 = 1,350,000 / 15,000,000 x 100 = 9%. The figure 11.1% comes from dividing sales by profit, which is the wrong way round.

questions.q: Fuel was used in the last week of June but the invoice arrives in July. How should the June report treat it?
o: Leave it out of June and report it in July when the invoice is received
Include an estimate of the cost in June and note that it is an estimate
Spread the cost equally across June and July so each month looks level
Leave it out of both months because the invoice amount is not yet known
questions.why: Costs belong in the period in which the fuel was used (cut-off). When the exact amount is not known, an estimate with a note is better than leaving a known cost out and overstating June's profit.

questions.q: What is the difference between the ledger and the ticketing system, and what should Garfield do first?
o: J$270,000; use the higher figure because it comes from the system
J$41,520,000; ignore it because small differences do not matter
J$81,000; take the average of the two figures for the report
J$270,000; trace the items to find the cause before reporting
questions.why: J$41,520,000 - J$41,250,000 = J$270,000. A reconciliation traces the difference (timing, a missing batch, a keying error), then corrects the records before the report is issued.

questions.q: How can Garfield best show that the revenue figure on the dashboard really came from the accounts?
o: Reference each figure to its ledger account or report, and note any adjustments
Print the dashboard and ask each depot clerk to sign it as correct and complete
Round every figure to the nearest J$100,000 so that small errors cannot show
Hide the formulas and lock the file so that no one can change the totals by mistake
questions.why: An audit trail ties each reported figure back to source documents so that it can be checked by someone else. Signatures, rounding and hidden formulas do not show where a figure came from.

questions.q: Several depot clerks enter data on the same spreadsheet. Which step best protects the accuracy of the totals?
o: Ask the clerks to email the sheet to each other after every change they make
Have the oldest clerk check every figure at the end of each month
Let each clerk change only their own data cells; lock formulas and log changes
Replace the spreadsheet with a paper form signed by each clerk every week
questions.why: Controlling who can change what, locking formulas and logging changes reduce errors and make them traceable. Passing copies around creates different versions, and a single end-of-month check cannot find errors that were overwritten.

questions.q: What was the supermarket's sales growth over the year?
questions.why: Growth = (58,500,000 - 52,000,000) / 52,000,000 x 100 = 6,500,000 / 52,000,000 x 100 = 12.5%. Dividing by this year's sales instead of last year's gives 11.1%, which is wrong.

questions.q: What are the supermarket's debtor days on its restaurant sales?
o: 35 days
28 days
12 days
95 days
questions.why: Credit sales per day = J$29,200,000 / 365 = J$80,000. Debtor days = J$2,800,000 / J$80,000 = 35 days. Compared with 30-day terms, restaurants are paying about five days late.

questions.q: The current ratio is 1.8 : 1 and the quick ratio is 1.2 : 1. Why is the quick ratio lower?
o: It leaves out cash, which is not available to pay bills
It adds the budget variance to current liabilities
It counts only the debts due after one year
It leaves out stock, which may take time to turn into cash
questions.why: Quick ratio = (current assets - stock) / current liabilities = (5,400,000 - 1,800,000) / 3,000,000 = 1.2. Stock is excluded because it must first be sold. A big gap means the firm relies on stock to cover short-term debts.

questions.q: By what percentage was the electricity cost over budget?
questions.why: Variance = J$3,456,000 - J$3,200,000 = J$256,000 over budget. Percentage = 256,000 / 3,200,000 x 100 = 8%. The percentage is based on the budget, not on the actual cost.

questions.q: Which display best shows how the budget is split among departments?
o: A line graph with one line for each department over a 12-month period
A pie chart or stacked bar, with the parts adding to 100%
A table of every journal entry made during the year in each department
A dial showing the total budget compared to last year's total only
questions.why: A pie chart or stacked bar shows how a whole divides into parts. A line graph shows a trend over time, and a table of journal entries is too detailed for a committee.

questions.q: What should a red flag on the dashboard mean?
o: The measure has been checked by two officers and is correct
The measure is within the target and no one needs to look at it
The figure has been estimated and will be corrected next month
The measure is outside the agreed tolerance and needs attention and action
questions.why: Red, amber and green show how a measure stands against agreed limits. Red means outside the tolerance. The limits must be agreed with the users in the specification so that everyone reads the colours the same way.

questions.q: What should each line of commentary in the committee's pack contain?
o: What changed, by how much, the cause, the effect and the proposed action
A repeat of every figure in the table above it, in the same order as the table
Only the total for the month, since the table already shows all the detail
A list of the officers who prepared the figures and their grades
questions.why: Commentary explains causes and consequences, so councillors who are not accountants can act. Repeating the table, or listing names, adds nothing. Plain language and explained terms are best.

questions.q: Complaints per 1,000 service users belongs to which perspective of a balanced scorecard?
o: Financial
Internal process
Customer
Learning and growth
questions.why: Complaints per 1,000 users show how customers see the service, which is the customer perspective. Financial measures show results for owners and funders, and learning and growth shows whether the organisation can keep improving.

questions.q: The manager asks the reporting officer to change the dates on invoices worth J$1,200,000. What should she do?
o: Change the dates but add a note in the pack so that the board is made aware of it
Change only half of the invoices, so that the effect on the quarter is smaller
Refuse, use the correct period and report the request upward if it continues
Say nothing and prepare the pack, since the manager is responsible for the figures
questions.why: Moving transactions to the wrong period distorts the results. A note does not make it honest. The officer must report accurately and, if pressed, refer the request to the finance director, the audit committee or internal audit.

questions.q: The officer wants to email the customer-account spreadsheet to her personal account to work from home. What is the best course?
o: Use secure remote access if approved, and never send customer data to personal email
Email it to herself, then delete the message from her inbox when she has finished
Print the whole spreadsheet and carry it home in her bag to work on there
Email it to herself but protect the file with a password made from her own name
questions.why: Customer data must be handled under the information policy and the data protection law, which require it to be kept secure and used for a proper purpose. Personal email, paper copies and weak passwords all lose control of the data.

questions.q: After the pack is issued, the officer finds that one dashboard figure is wrong by J$450,000. What should she do?
o: Wait to see if any manager notices before saying anything
Correct the figure in next month's pack and say nothing about this month
Delete the dashboard from the shared folder so that no one uses it
Tell the users promptly, issue the corrected figure and record the cause
questions.why: Errors found after issue should be reported at once so that decisions are not based on wrong data. Issue the correction, note the cause and improve the check so that it does not happen again.

questions.q: An organisation had an average of 45 staff during the year and 9 left. What was the staff turnover rate?
questions.why: Turnover = leavers / average staff x 100 = 9 / 45 x 100 = 20%. Dividing by 100 instead of the average number of staff gives a wrong answer.
